pages.text: The Niger and the Benue

image.note: Cover: two great rivers meeting in a Y across a map of Nigeria

pages.text: Contents. The Niger's Journey / The Benue / Where They Meet / Life on the River / The River to the Sea / The Two Great Rivers.

Nigeria takes its very name from a river: the mighty Niger. And the Niger has a great partner, the Benue, that joins it in the heart of the country. Together these two rivers water the land, feed millions, and carry the story of Nigeria itself. This is the tale of the two great rivers, and the country they made.

image.note: The Niger and Benue meeting in a Y across Nigeria

pages.text: A great river is more than water. It is a road, a farm, a fishing ground, and a home to countless creatures. The Niger and the Benue have shaped how people live across Nigeria for thousands of years. To follow them is to travel the length and breadth of the land.

image.note: Life gathered along a great river

pages.text: The Niger is one of the greatest rivers in all of Africa. But it does not begin in Nigeria at all. It rises far away, in the highlands of Guinea, near the western coast, as a small stream, and then sets out on an enormous journey.

image.note: The Niger's source as a small highland stream

pages.text: The Niger travels an astonishing path. It flows first away from the sea, north towards the edge of the great desert, then swings round in a huge curve, as if changing its mind, and turns back south again, at last entering Nigeria and flowing down through the heart of the land.

image.note: The Niger's great curving path across West Africa

pages.text: All along its long journey the Niger gathers strength, fed by rains and smaller streams, growing from a stream into a mighty river, wide and brown and powerful, carrying rich mud that makes the land along its banks green and good for farming.

image.note: The broad, powerful Niger flowing through Nigeria

pages.text: The Niger has a great partner: the Benue, the largest of all the rivers that flow into it. The Benue rises to the east, in the highlands of Cameroon, and flows westward across Nigeria, gathering its own waters as it comes, until it is a broad and powerful river in its own right.

image.note: The Benue rising in the eastern highlands

pages.text: For much of the year the Benue runs full and strong, and boats can travel along it, carrying people and goods across the country. Like the Niger, it brings life to the land it crosses, watering farms and filling fishing nets all along its banks.

image.note: Boats and farms along the Benue

pages.text: The two great rivers are travelling towards each other, the Niger from the west, the Benue from the east, and at last, in the very middle of Nigeria, at a town called Lokoja, they meet. It is one of the great sights of the country: two mighty rivers joining into one.

image.note: The confluence of the two rivers at Lokoja

pages.text: At the meeting place you can sometimes see the two waters flowing side by side before they mix, a little different in colour, one from the west and one from the east, joining into a single, even mightier river. From here, as one, they flow on together towards the distant sea.

image.note: The two waters meeting and mixing at the confluence

pages.text: It is from this great river that the whole country takes its name. Niger, and the land the river runs through: Nigeria. Every time you say the name of your country, you are naming the mighty river at its heart. The two rivers did not just shape the land. They named it.

image.note: The name Nigeria drawn from the river

pages.text: All along the two rivers, life gathers at the water's edge. Fishermen paddle out in narrow canoes and cast their nets, catching fish to feed their families and sell in the markets. The rivers have fed the people of this land for longer than anyone can remember.

image.note: Fishermen casting nets from canoes

pages.text: The rivers water the farms, too. When the rains come, the rivers rise and spread rich mud across the low land beside them, and there farmers grow rice and other crops in the fertile soil the river leaves behind. Where the great rivers flow, the land is green and giving.

image.note: Green farms along the fertile riverbank

pages.text: And the rivers are roads. Long before there were tarred highways, boats carried people and goods up and down the Niger and the Benue, from town to town. Even today, the rivers remain busy waterways, alive with boats, threading the country together.

image.note: Busy boats carrying goods along the river

pages.text: After Lokoja, the joined rivers flow on southward, growing ever broader, until they near the coast. And there the great river does something remarkable. It splits, into many channels, spreading out into a vast, watery maze of creeks and swamps and islands: the great Niger Delta.

image.note: The Niger splitting into the wide delta

pages.text: The delta is a rich and teeming place, thick with mangrove trees and creeks, alive with fish and birds, and home to many people. Through its countless channels, the water of the two great rivers, after its journey of thousands of miles, at last pours out into the ocean.

image.note: The teeming mangrove creeks of the delta

pages.text: So there they are: the Niger, born in the far highlands of Guinea and curving across half of West Africa, and the Benue, flowing in from the eastern hills, meeting at the heart of Nigeria and journeying on together to the sea. Two rivers, one great life-giving path across the land.

image.note: The full journey of both rivers, source to sea

pages.text: They water the farms, fill the nets, carry the boats, and give the country its very name. The next time you cross a river, or see one on a map, remember the two great rivers of Nigeria, flowing as they have for countless ages, through the heart of the land they made.

image.note: A child looking out over a great Nigerian river

pages.text: Words to know. The Niger: the great river that gives Nigeria its name. The Benue: the largest river that joins the Niger. Confluence: the place where two rivers meet, at Lokoja. Delta: the wide, split mouth where a river meets the sea. Source: the place where a river begins.

image.note: Labelled map of the Niger and the Benue

pages.text: The Niger and the Benue are Nigeria's own great rivers, but every land has its rivers, mountains, and wonders. From the frozen poles to the delta creeks, our world is shaped by water. Which part of it will you explore next?
